core: Working definition of pathophysiology (study of how disease changes normal function; MeSH-attributed)
Health as working balance vs disease as disruption
Five disease patterns: genetic, infectious, inflammatory, degenerative, traumatic (one line each + original example)
Signs vs symptoms distinction (observable vs felt)
Why nurses study pathophysiology (why guides what to watch; assessment first step of nursing process)
Honest framing: pathophysiology as the why behind every symptom, not a diagnostic crystal ball
supporting: Etiology as the cause or origin of disease
Acute vs chronic course (chronic = a year or more)
Screening finds disease before symptoms; early finding makes treatment easier
Fever as a sign, not a disease
outOfScope: Fluid and electrolyte balance (sibling topic fluid-and-electrolyte-basics)

claims.claim: Pathophysiology is the study of how disease changes the body's normal function; the National Library of Medicine's MeSH vocabulary frames the concept (physiopathology) as disordered function in disease states.
Health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO founding definition).

A sign is something found during a physical exam or as a result of a laboratory or imaging test that shows a person may have a condition; signs can be observed by a health care provider or other person, and examples include fever, swelling, skin rash, and high blood pressure.

A symptom is something a person feels or experiences that may indicate a disease or condition; symptoms can only be reported by the person experiencing them, do not show up on medical tests, and examples include pain, nausea, fatigue, and anxiety.
Etiology is the cause or origin of a disease.
A condition caused by variants in one or more genes is called a genetic disorder.

Infectious diseases are diseases caused by germs; the four main types of germs are bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and strep throat and urinary tract infections are common bacterial infections.
Inflammation occurs when the body releases chemicals that trigger an immune response to fight off infection or heal damaged tissue; chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs.

Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis; with osteoarthritis, the cartilage that pads the ends of bones breaks down and becomes rough, and sometimes all the cartilage wears away so the bones rub together.
A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; falling, twisting, or getting hit can cause a sprain, and ankle and wrist sprains are common.
Chronic diseases last a year or more and require ongoing medical attention or limit daily activities.
A fever is a body temperature higher than normal and is usually a sign that the body is trying to fight an illness or infection, not a disease itself.

The nursing process, the essential core of registered-nurse practice, begins with assessment — a systematic, dynamic way to collect and analyze data about a client, the first step in delivering nursing care.
Screening looks for disease before a person has symptoms; when a disease is found early it may be easier to treat or cure, while by the time symptoms appear it may have grown and spread.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The working definition of pathophysiology: the NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms currently has no entry for 'pathophysiology' (the definition page returns a not-found state), so a consumer-accessible NCI definition could not be verified at research time.
positions: The National Library of Medicine's MeSH thesaurus defines the concept (qualifier physiopathology/pathophysiology) with the scope note 'used with organs and diseases for disordered function in disease states.'

Older consumer glossaries describe pathophysiology as 'the study of changes in normal body functions caused by disease,' but no current authoritative page carrying that wording could be fetched and verified.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines pathophysiology as the study of how disease changes the body's normal function and attributes the concept to the MeSH scope note (disordered function in disease states). The NCI dictionary is cited only for terms it actually defines: sign, symptom, etiology, and inflammation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Disease-pattern taxonomies vary across textbooks; some add immune, neoplastic, or metabolic patterns beyond the five in this lesson.
positions: This lesson's brief names five patterns: genetic, infectious, inflammatory, degenerative, and traumatic.
Other texts list additional patterns such as immune or neoplastic diseases.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson covers the five named patterns, does not claim the list is exhaustive, and points to the cellular-injury and inflammation sibling topics for the mechanisms underneath.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only boilerplate ('Pathophysiology Basics is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations...') with no substantive factual claims; nothing from it was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft with an original, source-verified lesson.
Anchored the working definition to the NLM MeSH scope note after confirming the NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms no longer serves a pathophysiology entry.
Kept every clinical claim (patterns, signs/symptoms, timeline, examples) tied to named Tier A sources; no invented numbers or unverified clinical specifics.
Distributed question keys across A/B/C/D with at least one C and one D per the subject's source-map cautions.

sourceRecords.title: How can gene variants affect health and development? (MedlinePlus Genetics)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; page title 'How can gene variants affect health and development?: MedlinePlus Genetics'). Verified: when a variant alters a protein that plays a critical role in the body, it can disrupt normal development or cause a health condition, and a condition caused by variants in one or more genes is called a genetic disorder. Supports the genetic disease pattern and the cystic fibrosis illustration (a well-known single-gene disorder). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Infectious Disease (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Verified: infectious diseases are diseases that are caused by germs; the four main types of germs are bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites; bacteria are one-celled germs that multiply quickly; strep throat and urinary tract infections are common bacterial infections. Supports the infectious pattern, the strep throat example, and the urinary tract infection used in the signs/symptoms example. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Osteoarthritis (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Verified: osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis; in a healthy joint the ends of the bones are covered with smooth, slippery cartilage that pads the bones and helps them glide; with osteoarthritis the cartilage breaks down and becomes rough, and sometimes all the cartilage wears away and the bones rub together. Supports the degenerative pattern and the gradual-onset example. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the traumatic pattern, the sprained-ankle example, and the sudden-onset line. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
